thought_title: Jewish food laws, Sabbath, circumcision, and calendar observance are absurd
orientation: The author has just dismissed pagan idolatry and Jewish sacrificial worship; now he turns to the remaining Jewish practices—food rules, Sabbath, circumcision, and calendar observance—arguing that Diognetus does not need to be taught how ridiculous they are.
pass_a_gloss: But indeed the timidity about their foods and the superstition about the Sabbaths and the boastfulness of circumcision and the pretense of fasting and new moon observance, laughable things and worthy of no account, I do not think you need to learn from me. For of the things created by God for the use of humans, to accept some as having been created well, but to reject others as useless and superfluous—how is this not unlawful? And to speak falsely of God as forbidding on the day of the Sabbaths to do something good—how is this not impious? And to boast of the mutilation of the flesh as a proof of election, as though because of this they were especially loved by God—how is this not worthy of mockery? And that they, attending to stars and moon, make the observance of months and days and divide up the arrangements of God and the changes of seasons according to their own impulses, some for festivals, others for mournings—who would consider this a proof of piety and not much more of foolishness? That Christians rightly abstain from the common folly and deceit and from the meddlesomeness and boastfulness of the Jews, I think you have learned sufficiently; but the mystery of their own piety, do not expect to be able to learn from a human being.

choices.why: The word means fearfulness or skittishness about a thing; 'timidity' captures the anxious scrupulosity about foods without importing modern religious vocabulary.
In this context it denotes the sham or dissembling character of fasting and new-moon observance, not Socratic irony; 'pretense' keeps the negative force.
The author uses a deliberately reductive term for circumcision; 'mutilation' preserves the polemical edge, while 'flesh' keeps the physical connotation.
The verb means to make a boastful claim; 'to boast' is direct and keeps the active, self-aggrandizing force.
The noun denotes officious, intrusive busyness; 'meddlesomeness' captures the negative connotation of prying into matters beyond one's proper sphere.
The term denotes a secret known only to initiates; 'mystery' preserves the sense that Christian piety cannot be learned from a human source.

pass_b_english: But as for their timidity about foods, their superstition about the Sabbath, their boasting about circumcision, and their pretense about fasting and the new moon, these things are laughable and not worth a word. I do not think you need to learn about them from me.
For when God created things for human use, how is it not forbidden to accept some of them as well made but to reject others as useless and superfluous?
And how is it not impious to tell lies about God, as though he forbids doing something good on the Sabbath day?
And how is it not worthy of mockery to boast that the mutilation of the flesh is a mark of election, as though they are for this reason especially loved by God?

And who would consider it a sign of piety rather than of great foolishness to sit attending to the stars and the moon, keeping watch over months and days, and to divide up God's arrangements and the changes of the seasons according to their own impulses, some for festivals and some for times of mourning?

So I think you have learned sufficiently how rightly Christians keep away from the common folly and deceit and from the meddlesomeness and boasting of the Jews. But do not expect to be able to learn the mystery of their own piety from any human being.

problems.quote: to accept some of them as well made and to reject others as useless and superfluous—how is that not forbidden?
problems.why: The logic is inverted; the author seems to be criticizing Jewish food laws but the phrasing suggests God's creation is at fault.
problems.fix: Rephrase to clarify that Jews, not God, are declaring some foods unacceptable.

fixed: The logic is not inverted: the source says 'to accept some as having been created well, but to reject others as useless and superfluous—how is this not unlawful?' The English already says the same thing. The criticism is of those who reject some of God's created things, not of God's creation itself. No change needed beyond the existing wording.

polish.changed: Clarified the rhetorical questions by moving the interrogative phrase earlier in each sentence, so the criticism of Jewish food laws reads naturally as a question about rejecting God's creation rather than as an inverted statement. Also broke the first long sentence into two for easier reading aloud.
